subtopic: SHIPMENT OF GRAIN THROUGH PORT CHURCHILL

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SHIPMENT OF GRAIN THROUGH PORT CHURCHILL
speechtext:
I wish
to ask a question of the Minister of Railways. It is based on an article which appeared in the Journal on Saturday under the following heading:
2,000,000 bushel wheat shipment for north route.
Saskatchewan pool announces Churchill will get big business during the summer.
Did the Minister of Railways receive any official notice of such shipment? If so, did he receive it in time to enable him to make the necessary arrangements? Has he any idea how many cargoes such a shipment would make?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways) :
speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: SHIPMENT OF GRAIN THROUGH PORT CHURCHILL
speechtext:
Due to the item in the press regarding Churchill, I expected that someone would ask as to details and, therefore, I may state that the item mentioned is based on fact.
As I advised the house some weeks ago, the Department of Railways and Canals has been doing everything possible to encourage a proper test during the coming season of the Churchill route, and about ten days ago a representative of a responsible grain company called upon me and made a verbal proposal to send 2,000,000 bushels of grain to the Churchill elevator on condition that the government would not make any charge for elevation or storage. I requested that he put his proposal in writing, which he did, and the matter was then discussed with the department of Trade and Commerce, the Board of Grain Commissioners and the officers of my own denartment. As a result of these

Wheat Pool
discussions a satisfactory agreement has been drawn up between the Department of Railways and Canals and the grain company mentioned permitting the grain company to ship 2,000,000 bushels of grain forthwith to the Churchill elevator, the understanding being that they ship out from that port at least 1,000,000 bushels during the coming season. The grain company undertake also that in the event of other exporters shipping through Churchill they will lend such exporters any reasonable shortage to fill their boats and not charge a premium in excess of one-half cent per bushel for such loan. The borrower, however, must show evidence satisfactory to the Board of Grain Commissioners that he has provided for the full shipment that he is making.
The grain elevator has a 2,000,000 bushel storage capacity and a 500,000 bushel work house capacity. Therefore, even with the elevator storage space completely filled, grain can still be moved through the elevator directly from cars to ships. The permission, therefore, to the grain company mentioned for the use of 2,000,000 bushels storage space does not in any way prevent other shippers from using the port.
In order to prevent congestion of grain at Churchill and at the suggestion of the Board of Grain Commissioners, a permit system, similar to that in effect at Vancouver, will be put on, and grain will be allowed into Churchill only under these permits, as and when vessel tonnage has been provided or storage space available. The railways and the exporters are all familiar with the operation of this permit system, which has now been used for six or seven years in connection with the port of Vancouver.
I am informed that 1,250,000 bushels has been already purchased by the grain company, and a movement to the Churchill elevator will probably begin within the next fortnight. The operation of the Churchill elevator within the next ten days has been arranged for, and I see no reason why this whole movement cannot be made without any trouble whatsoever.
The government has been making every effort to have the insurance rates out of Churchill lowered, and I think that I may safely say that there is likely to be a slight lowering of the insurance rates out of Churchill this season; at least we are very hopeful of this because of certain information which we have received. The fact that the charges for elevation and storage are eliminated, as they were last year, naturally cancels a good deal of the excess insurance, though, of course, 41761-185	[DOT]
it will be understood that the port of Churchill ultimately will have to operate on the same basis as other ports of the dominion.
May I add in conclusion that every effort is being made by my department, and such efforts have been going on continuously, to have the Churchill route given a fairly complete test in every way during the season of 1932.
The hon. member asked about the number of cargoes. I should judge that 2,000,000 bushels would be in the neighbourhood of eight cargoes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Income War Tax Act to provide that the members of the judiciary, and the members of the military, naval and air forces of Canada and of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, other than enlisted men, shall be liable to pay a special income tax of ten per cent upon their salaries received during the fiscal year 1932-33, in addition to any other tax payable under the act.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBEES OP MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I explained to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) would proceed with this resolution in order to get it into committee and through first reading, but that full opportunity would be given to the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) to discuss the matter at some future date.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. LaVergne in the chair.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBEES OP MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES
speechtext:
I take it that this resolution is to be read in conjunction with Bill No. 19. Am I right in assuming that the object of the resolution is to provide for some contribution to be made by those who are mentioned to help defray the expenses of government in a manner similar to that being

done by members of the public service from whose salaries a ten per cent deduction is being made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBEES OP MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES
speechtext: My right hon. friend is quite correct. A grave question existed as to whether or not we had the right to deduct from the salaries of the classes mentioned, but, as I understand it, there is no question of our having the right to tax. By this method we are accomplishing that which is being done by Bill No. 19 with respect to other members of the public service.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBEES OP MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES
speechtext: Are we to take it that the government has changed its point of view as to the desirability of a contribution being made by those who come within the categories here set forth. As I understood the former discussion the question was not so much one of the legal authority to ask for a contribution from those here enumerated but rather that it was thought that persons belonging to these particular classes should not be called upon to make a contribution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBEES OP MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES
speechtext: There was a question in the case of the judges as to whether or not this ought to be done. As was intimated on a previous occasion by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), we have received evidence that members of the service and, in certain instances, members of the judiciary wish to make a contribution similar to that being made by other members of the public service.

subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBEES OP MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES
speechtext: Will the minister advise the committee just what is meant by the words "in addition to any other tax payable under the act"? I should like to understand the position of those officials who are already contributing to the Income War Tax Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBEES OP MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES
speechtext: As will be made clear when the bill is introduced, this resolution provides for a reduction equivalent to the deduction of ten per cent being made in the case of other members of the public service. This tax will be in addition to any amounts paid as income tax, as provided for by the statute already existing.

subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBEES OP MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES
speechtext: Some of these individuals already pay a tax and some do not, that is the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBEES OP MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES
speechtext: If they do not pay a tax they will not be affected by this provision.

subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBEES OP MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the committee already knows my views with regard to this whole matter. I am opposed to any reduction in the salaries of judges or any other

Income War Tax Act
officials but I do think that if a reduction is to be made it should be made under the provisions of Bill No. 19. The government in its wisdom has seen fit to introduce a special resolution to amend the Income War Tax Act which covers members of the judiciary, the military, naval and air forces, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, but, in my opinion, there are other classes which should come under the provisions of this resolution or of Bill No. 19. The first class to which I refer is the lieutenant-governors, which should contribute just the same as the lightkeepers, the judges and members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. To use a Scotch expression, there should be no stepbairns in our family. In my opinion, this class should suffer in the interests of the dominion just the same as the judges, the charwomen, the lighthouse keepers or other members of the public service.
If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) does not see fit to amend Bill No. 19, I submit that this resolution should also cover those judges who have been retired and who are now receiving pensions. Many of these judges are receiving large pensions and they should suffer a ten per cent reduction during 1932. I tried to look up the figures but was unable to locate them and consequently my information may not be accurate, but I understand one judge is receiving a pension of $12,000 per year, and is still doing business with the law firm with which he is connected. If I remember correctly, other judges are receiving pensions of 89,000 per year and are able to carry on in their legal practices. Other judges are receiving other amounts. Whether the Minister of Finance, in his judgment, thinks this action should be taken under this resolution or under Bill No. 19, every man or woman in this country who is receiving any money from the public treasury should be treated in the same manner; no distinction should be made. I am opposed to the whole principle of the proposal; in my view it is a mistake to make any deductions from salaries of judges, members of parliament, charwomen, lighthouse keepers, or anyone else receiving money from the government, but if the reduction must be made, everyone should be treated alike, and judges who are receiving large pensions should come under this resolution or under Bill No. 19.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBEES OP MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES
speechtext:
The hon member for
Antigonish-Guysborough has made his position very clear to-day as he has done on previous occasions; he has left no doubt in our minds as to what is in his with respect to this matter. I must repeat: This is not a salary 4X761-1851
reduction; I must insist respectfully on using the word "deduction." We are asking for a contribution for one year. My hon. friend should not treat this as if we were reducing salaries. While I have no doubt, as always happens in a measure of general application, there will be individual cases of great hardship, on the whole I believe that those who are affected by this resolution, as well as those who come under the provisions of Bill No. 19, are prepared in these very difficult times to join with other elements in the country in making reasonable contributions to the federal treasury.
I must respectfully take issue with my hon. friend when he attempts to place the nine representatives in Canada of His Majesty the King upon the same basis as other civil servants; I think they stand in a class altogether different. While the question may be arguable, I do not think it is a subject upon which we should enlarge, especially under these circumstances and at this time.
With respect to the question which was raised by my hon. friend, let me say this: We have touched no pension and if we attempted to make a deduction from the pensions of judges, we would be discriminating against them rather than discriminating in their favour, as he apparently has in mind we are doing because we have not attempted to make deductions in the case of judges. My hon. friend has instanced the case of one judge who is in receipt of a pension of $12,000 a year, and states that that judge is in addition engaged in private practice. My hon. friend must not attempt to prove a general rule by a single instance. That judge, under the terms upon which he went to the bench, is entitled to that pension; he has a right to it in virtue of the statute provided in that behalf. But I must point out to my hon. friend that that judge who is in receipt of his pension of $12,000 a year makes his contribution as an income tax payer. Unless and until we came to the time in Oanada when we were prepared to reduce pensions, it would be manifestly unjust to single out the judges for adverse treatment in that respect.

subtopic: SPECIAL TAX ON INCOMES OP JUDGES AND MEMBEES OP MILITARY, NAVAL, AIR AND POLICE FORCES
speechtext:
Just upon that point, not only in the present debate but also in previous ones, the Minister of Finance stated that this was not a reduction in salary; that it was a contribution by the civil servants of this country to get over a situation for which perhaps none of us is to blame. I was always of opinion that a contribution was voluntary; a contribution was never something which was forced from one. If you, sir, want to give
Income War Tax Act

$500 to build a new church in your constituency, you give it voluntarily; but if somebody, for instance the legislature of Quebec or the federal parliament, passes a law compelling you to do that, then I cannot understand how the Minister of Finance can call that a contribution. Surely he does not mean to say that the poor women who come here at five o'clock in the morning and whom I meet returning home every day when I come here at seven o'clock in the morning, are willing contributors to this reduction of ten per cent. In view of the fact that the government has been compelled to introduce this legislation with regard to judges, the Minister of Finance cannot say that the judges are willing to contribute ten per cent of their salaries. Moreover, the Prime Minister has told us-and I hope I am not misquoting him; perhaps I shall say we inferred from his statement- and he cannot take objection to what I am saying-that he was communicating with the judges in an endeavour to get them to agree to this reduction. Perhaps the government are to be commended to a certain extent for making a right-about face on this matter of exemptions from the ten per cent cut. During the debates that took place in committee on this ten per cent cut, it was pointed out by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice, and to some extent but not quite so forcibly, by the Minister of National Revenue, that it was impossible to include the judges in the ten per cent cut. I will be fair to the Minister of Justice and say that when he spoke in this house on March 6 last, as reported on page 831 of Hansard, he argued at length that the judiciary should be exempted from any cut in regard to salary, but before he sat down he said that perhaps a tax could be imposed. Apparently, Mr. Chairman, the government led by the right hon. the Prime Minister, were bound and determined a month ago that the judges should be exempt from the ten per cent cut as well as the army and navy officers and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. But now they make a right-about turn, and they do not do it very gracefully. I see no reason why these positions should not have been included in the bill in the first place, but now the government is bringing them in, not by the front door, not even by the side door, but in a camouflaged way by the back door, by an additional ten per cent income tax. I do not altogether object to that. I stated before in this house, and I state again, that I have always been of the opinion that there should be no exemptions from this ten per cent cut *-judges, army officers, naval officers and Royal Canadian Mounted Police-and I am still of that opinion. The government should never have attempted to make these exemptions. I should like to quote the remarks of the Prime Minister concerning the exemption of officers of the permanent force. Hansard contains his argument as to why those officers should not receive the ten per cent cut in their pay. At this point may I say I am not

particular as to whether it is called a deduction or a tax. Hansard for April 6 of this year, at page 1776, contains the following statement by the right hon. gentleman:
We come to the third of the three classes, the crown, the judiciaries and the forces of the crown. The men who come within this third class are under discipline-they cannot resign even if they so desire. They are not under an ordinary contract, they are enlisted men, and the government contracts that during the term of their enlistment they shall receive a given compensation. It is not a contract in the ordinary sense because the word "enlistment" is used rather than the word "contract." They cannot leave the service without being guilty of desertion and prosecution, and they cannot resign.
Those were the words of the Prime Minister, and with all due respect to him I say he was wrong in his facts in regard to contracts made with officers of the permanent force. I am about to quote from the attestation paper which every officer and man who enlists in the permanent force must sign. Questions appear on this paper to which answers must be given, and an affidavit has to be taken before a justice of the peace or a magistrate. Question No. 17 on this document is as follows:
Are you willing to enlist or reengage under such conditions as to pay and service as may be authorized and laid down from time to time by the governor in council?
The answer to that question must be "Yes," or the applicant would not be taken on the force. I say that in the first place there was no reason why the officers of the permanent force should not have been included in the ten per cent cut. However the Prime Minister and the members of the government are at all times very loath to admit that they have erred in judgment. There is no doubt, however, that they did err in connection with the exemptions they allowed from the cut. Now, in a roundabout way they are introducing legislation to provide an additional ten per cent income tax. I am not familiar with enforcement of the law in connection with this imposed tax, and although I cannot make a definite statement, I think I can see where a good deal of litigation may arise from the imposition of the additional ten per cent income tax on salaries of judges, army officers and members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
I do not know whether the Minister of Justice and his law officers have seen daylight enough to know that the proposed cut is legal. There is no doubt however that the proposed legislation is by no means direct, and may turn out to be a great expense to the government and the country. There was

never any satisfactory argument advanced by the government in regard to the exemption. Not one government follower, with the exception of three or four members of the cabinet, got up and defended the ten per cent cut, so far as exemptions were concerned. Hon. members across the floor say they were consulted in regard to the ten per cent reduction in indemnities. I do not agree with the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough in regard to the ten per cent cut in the salaries of civil servants, or the indemnities of members of the House of Commons and the Senate. I think, perhaps, owing to conditions throughout the country the cut was necessary. I do say however that once this government attempted class legislation and the exemption of certain classes auch as judges, army officers and Royal Canadian Mounted Police they were playing a very dangerous game. This is no time for class legislation; there should have been no exemptions in the first place. Now, with no grace and not admitting that they erred in judgment, the government brings in the legislation which is before us.
To the Minister of Finance I pay the tribute that I never heard him defend the exemptions. He listened carefully to the remarks made by hon. members on this side of the house, and did not attempt to defend the government's attitude. On the other hand, the Minister of Justice attempted a defence, and at all times the Prime Minister on a high and mighty plane said that we must leave these gentlemen alone, and that their salaries must not be cut. Now, however, we find that legislation is brought in for an extra ten per cent income tax. The legislation we had before us earlier in the session was hasty, and discriminated in favour of certain classes. That is a bad thing for any government and any country.

As the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) has stated, the claim that the men enlisted for a specific rate of pay during the currency of their enlistment- which I would certainly agree to being good law is no longer tenable, because, as he stated, there is a question on the attestation paper, number 17, by which they specifically agree to enlist for such pay and allowance as may be authorized and allowed from time to time.
I am advised that that was put in some six or seven years ago to meet just such a case as we have before us; and as enlistments are for only a three-year period, all enlisted men now in the service must have subscribed to 
that question number 17. Therefore by the terms of their enlistment they agreed to take such pay as was then current or might afterwards be arranged. They cannot resign, it is true, but a.t the end of every three years they have the opportunity of not reenlisting, and at any time they can buy themselves out for a moderate sum. I know that, because I did it myself. I am not objecting to these enlisted men being exempted because of the amount of their pay, which, as the minister says is not large. I am objecting to their being exempted because they are soldiers or enlisted men. It is an unsound principle. If he said, as he should say, in Bill No. 19, that all below a certain salary shall be exempt, I would be heartily with him. Let me compare two classes of men. I am not going into details unless they are asked for, but I have them here. I have worked it out that ordinary married soldiers get by way of pay and allowances well over $100 a month-as a matter of fact Sill, but I may have overstated some of the allowances. In addition, they have the chance of promotion, which is very considerable, for the first step up means an increase in pay of something like 25 per cent and then it goes rapidly on from there. They also have the prospect of a pension to which they are not asked to contribute. That is a substantial increment. Compare the position of those men with that of a class that come more home to myself, the men who are working on government lighthouse tenders, government patrol boats, and lifeboats. They get $90 a month, from which is deducted ten per cent, leaving $81. Let me take a married man in this case also. A man working on one of these boats has to keep his wife and family on shore, so that he has to maintain a house and pay rent, and of course provide food and medical attendance for his wife. He gets no pension, and the prospect of promotion is so very small that it is negligible. He is taxed ten per cent, while any of these enlisted men, with these considerable advantages over this man, get well over $100 a month and are not taxed.
To illustrate my argument. Under section 5 of the bill the government have realized that it is not quite fair to tax the lowest paid employees ten per cent, and they have provided that as to those getting less than $1,200 a year, their contribution of five per cent under the superannuation act shall be paid by the government out of the consolidated revenue fund. So the government recognize that there is something that calls for help when men get less than $1,200 a year-a salary that one might describe as being wholly needful to

Income War Tax Act
provide necessities rather than luxuries. This paying of their superannuation fees for them, works out just the same as if those getting $1,200 and under were not subject to more than a five per cent deduction in their salaries. Why, instead of putting in that complicated machinery the government has not said that those people getting $1,200 and less would be taxed only five per cent, I do not know, but that would be only fair and just. As a matter of fact, I would make the lower salaries totally exempt. But it is unjust, it is unfair, it is illogical that men on the boats, who are not eligible to pay to the superannuation fund and who get this miserable $90 a month, $25 of which goes to their mess, leaving them only $65 to maintain their families, should be subject to a deduction of ten per cent, while those men getting not more than $1,200 a year who happen to pay superannuation get off with a deduction of five per cent. If the soldiers come under the $1,200 category, and as they do not pay to the superannuation fund, then by all means exempt them only five per cent. Or better still, put them all on the same basis, and simply say: If a civil servant is getting less than $1,200 he will be subject to a deduction of only five per cent. Then there could be no complaint. As it is, I do not think it is right that these enlisted men who are secure in their positions, which are well paid as such positions go, and who have the prospect of promotion and the certainty of pension, should be exempt while men who are receiving less money and less in the way of privileges should have to pay ten per cent, as in the cases I have mentioned. Of course, this particular clause in Bill No. 19 has not yet come before us, and I can onfy hope that the government will see its way to amend it as I have indicated. Hon. ministers opposite, however, heard all the arguments that were made when the resolution was in committee and they have brought in the bill as it stands, so that it does not look as if they intend to change it. I submit that it is not fair; it is not just nor equitable as between these two classes I have mentioned, the soldier and the other man on the boats- men who have greater responsibilities and less privilege and who are taxed ten per cent.

My salary is only $16.58 per month and now the ten per cent taken will leave it at $14.92.

because, after all, a post office in a small district renders valuable service, and these postmasters or postmistresses are accustomed, in order to accommodate the public, to give out mail at all hours. In many cases they are women who have no other means of support; I know of several of that class in my constituency. Surely the government does not think it fair and is not going to take the ten per cent from that class. I do not want to delay the measure, but I would ask the Minister of Finance, before this bill goes through, to give further consideration to those people. speechtext:
I want, just for a
moment, to refer to the question of rental allowances. My reason for doing so is that so many hundreds come under this provision and the department should make a definite ruling covering all those people and not leave the question to one of individual cases. I have received many communications, not only from individual postmasters, but from officials of the provincial bodies, and their complaint is a very real one, because they already have had the deduction made in their remuneration, which falls under three different classes: the salaries which they receive; the rental allowance which is paid to them, and certain allowances out of which they pay for heating, lighting and assistance, all of which are subject to the ten per cent reduction. Some of them own their own quarters for which they receive rental allowances, but many of them are renting buildings for post office purposes, paying the rent and then being in receipt of a rental allowance to cover the amount in lieu of the government providing the necessary accommodation. They have already had the deduction made in the rental allowance, while they have not been able to obtain a reduction in the rent they have to pay; they are paying the same rent as before which in some cases equals and in many cases exceeds the amount they formerly received in the way of rental allowances. They are unable to reduce the cost of maintenance and upkeep, heating, lighting and the paying for assistance, but the ten per cent reduction has taken place in the allowance given to them for those purposes. I have examined into the matter with some care in some twenty or twenty-five cases and I have found the actual reduction 
amounts to over 20 per cent upon their salaries, because the reduction applies to the rental allowance, where they still had to pay the same rent, furnishing the other ten per cent out of their own pocket, out of their salary, and it applies to the heating, lighting, assistance and other things, the cost of which was not reduced in any way and where again they had to make up the difference out of their salary. The actual result, which I am sure was not the intention of the government, was, as I say, that the reduction in their salary amounted on the average to over 20 per cent.
' As hundreds come under that class it is obvious that they should not be dealt with as individual cases, and after individual application on the part of those postmasters, but that the whole situation should be examined into and a definite rule laid down in respect of rental allowance, allowances made for maintenance and upkeep of building and for the provision of the assistance which is necessary. At the same time I may point out that they have already had those deductions made; they have already received their cheques minus that amount and they are complaining with, I think, some justice. A great deal of discrimination is involved. Let us take the case of the men who are working in a government-owned building. They receive no rent allowance; they pay no rent and of course they suffer no ten per cent reduction in that regard. Therefore there is a discrimination in their favour as against those who are renting a building owned by someone else or those who own their own building. There are these three classes, and the government might lay down a general rule in respect of each of them.

May I take a few moments of the time of the committee to deal with this question of rentals? So far as the post office is concerned, judging from the experience that I have had as the head of that department for a number of years, considerable complications arise in the matter of the rental allowed. For instance, there is the rental allowance paid to the postmaster, and based on revenue, where the post office is stationed in his own residence. Then there is the more important post office in the rural districts where the postmaster is allowed a certain allowance for a building outside when his own building is not a suitable place for the post office and where the allowance does not come up to the amount asked by the owner of the building. In such a case his allowance is supplemented by a vote from the Department of Public Works. What are you going to do in a case of that kind? Here you have an allowance to the postmaster based on the revenue from his office, and under the law and the regulations the Post Office Department cannot increase that allowance because it is based on revenue, but the Department of Public Works supplements that allowance with, say $50 annually. What are you going to do in such a case? My suggestion to the minister would be not to have the ten per cent deduction apply to any rental allowance except where, under the Civil Service Act, it is stated in the advertisement when vacancies are advertised that the allowance is to be taken as part of the salary. If that principle was adopted of not touching these rental allowances at all, I think that the minister would find that the deduction would be applied in a more equitable manner.
While I am on my feet, might I draw the attention of the minister to this other matter? In the Post Office Department there is what is called a forwarding allowance. That is to say, in a certain number of districts the mail from outside comes to a central office, and there it is re-sorted and distributed to the outlying small post offices, and the postmaster is allowed what is known as a forwarding allowance, which, of course, adds to his remuneration. I would suggest that the minister when dealing with the rental allowance might also deal with the forwarding allowance, and not have the ten per cent deduction apply to the forwarding allowance. These matters I think could be covered by the regulations. If the minister would make a note of this matter, it might be dealt with by the treasury board as they deem best.
The last time this bill was up I mentioned the case of those who are receiving their maximum salary for the class in which they are working, and who would be receiving a bonus of five per cent, if I might use that term, because the government is absorbing five per cent of the amount they contribute

There is another question. I brought it up when the bill was up before and perhaps the minister would tell me something about it or it if will be taken into consideration. I refer to those who are contributing to the retirement fund, comprising about 550 or 575, instead of to the superannuation fund. They do not get the benefit of this bonus which those who are contributing to the superannuation fund get! As I understand it, and I think I am right, those who contribute to the retirement fund pay in five per cent of their salary and the government contributes nothing, whereas those contributing to the superannuation fund pay in five per cent of their salary and the government adds whatever is necessary to maintain the superannuation fund. The minister will see the discrimination between the two classes, that a bonus of five per cent is granted in the case of those contributing to the superannuation fund and nothing in the case of those contributing to the retirement fund. I leave those suggestions with the minister because I do not wish to delay the passage of the bill.

Members of the House of Commons received foi the months of February, March and April the sum of $1,740, without any deduction. However that is not my chief point. It is quite likely that the 1933 session will commence and some payments will be made within the prescribed time of the one year's reduction. There has been some talk, in fact, that there may be a fall session. I am pleased the hon.
member for Kindersley has raised the question which I believe was considered previously in committee. The indemnities to the members of the House of Commons and the Senate are in an entirely different position from salaries to other persons. It is true that we can draw at the rate of $20 per day during the session, but if the session extends a period of fifty days, under statute the indemnity for that session is $4,000. It was our intention that the deduction should be made upon the indemnity for this session and this session only. That is to say, we intend that the members of the House of Commons and the Senate shall receive the sums of $3,600 by way of indemnity for this one session, and no more. I have before me an amendment which I will ask the Minister of National Revenue to move, and I believe it will clear the point beyond question. The amendment is as follows:
That section 3 be amended by adding the following as subsection (3): Notwithstanding the provisions of subsections (1) and (2) of this section the said deduction from the indemnity of members of the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada shall apply to such indemnity only for the session of parliament which commenced on the fourth day of February, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-two.
That would seem to answer the question of my hon. friend as to what might happen in the event of a fall session.

The object is simply to put into one issue, so to speak, the question of reduction of salaries of $1,200 and under. The effect would be that all those in receipt of a salary of $1,200 and under would be subject to a deduction of five per cent only. It would clarify the situation and save disputes, some of which have already begun as between the superannuation fund and the various retirement funds. The minister has indicated that he has already had to propose an amendment to meet objection by one of the members sitting to my right. There are several of these retirement funds and in some cases they differ considerably as between one and another. There will be endless disputes as to the rights of individuals. I would also say, in answer to the minister, that these deductions for superannuation are not penalties exacted from the civil servant; he gets value in return. In every case the government pays a sum equivalent to what he has contributed, and the man on retirement, or his dependents on his death, will get the benefit. So that if a man out of his $1,000 spends $50 in contributions to the superannuation fund, it cannot be argued that he is being penalized because, as I have said, he is getting value. As the act reads to-day, with that later clause, No. 5, it discriminates against a class of persons drawing small salaries, who do not happen to be privileged to contribute to the fund. The answer is that the man who pays into the fund knows that the future of his wife and his family is provided for to that extent, while the man who is not allowed to contribute to the fund is conscious of that lack of protection against future events. There is always that Nemesis he must bear in mind. Out of his meagre salary he has to pay $80 or $100 for insurance, whereas the other man makes a deal with the government, who contributes fifty per cent of what he has to pay into the superannuation fund for similar protection. So that they are on a par. It does not matter what the man does with his $50, whether he contributes to a fund or buys insurance. It cannot be argued that this is at all fair. I see the minister consulting the Minister of Justice, and he will no doubt rise to a point of order and say that I am affecting the revenues of the crown and therefore out of order. Item agreed to.
Adjustment of War Claims - National Defence-militia services, $82,000; naval services, $500.
This has nothing to do with the adjustment of claims of individuals for reparations, I presume.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No, this item has to deal with deferred separation allowances and gratuities of members of the forces.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Naval service-to provide for the maintenance of the ships and establishments of the naval service, including the Royal Canadian Navy, the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve and the Roval Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve, $2,462,000.

I think we should
have some explanation of the operations of our navy in the last few months. What do these ships do from month to month? Even since parliament assembled we had our navy interfering with activities in several foreign ports. What instructions are given to the navy? I should like the minister to explain this item.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I do not know
whether the hon. gentleman has a particular incident in mind. As to the general operations, training goes on both on the east coast and on the west coast, and in the winter months it is customary for the boats to proceed to warmer waters and carry on the training there. That is general with all navies. In the summer, of course, our ships are in our northern waters, on the west coast up around the island, and on the east coast they spend part of their time in the St. Lawrence.

Is the purpose of
these ships simply to afford some sort of training? I had the idea that they were really patrol boats of a sort. That was the im-

pression given to us several years ago when the original expenditure -was under review. Now it seems these boats have been transformed into training ships, that they carry on training in the warmer waters as well as around our own coasts. Are these training ships or patrol boats?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Certainly they are
training ships, and there was never anything else intended. There are four destroyers, and the destroyer is essentially a combatant boat, for offensive or defensive purposes as required. The training cannot be done in our northern waters in winter, and it is customary in all nations for the boats in winter time to go to warmer waters. Some of the British boats, for instance, go to the Mediterranean in winter, and the Atlantic squadron is around the West Indies. It costs no more to have our ships move into warmer waters than to have them stay here and train.
What guns do these destroyers carry?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They vary. The two new destroyers, the Skeena and the Saguenay, are armed with 4-5 guns, if my memory serves me. I can say that they are armed as strongly as any destroyers in the world. As the hon. member may know, the Saguenay and the Skeena are the last word in destroyers. They came into commission last year, having been under process of construction a couple of years before. The other two, namely the Vancouver and the Champlain, are older boats, dating from the war period. The armament on them is not as heavy as on the other two. However, we have four very capable boats.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Permanent force, $4,844,000.

I should like to
make a few remarks with regard to this item, especially in view of the Disarmament conference now being held at Geneva. I am well aware of the fact that Canada has no very large armaments, and for that we ought to be thankful. At the same time, we do maintain a certain force, and at least once a year I think we ought to stop to consider whether or not we are in line with the developments which some day may possibly carry the world away from armaments.
I think once before this year I drew attention to a statement made by the Minister of Justice at a session of the Assembly of the League of Nations held at Geneva on September 9 of last year:	He said:
The armaments of Canada are practically negligible. We maintain only such military, naval and air forces as are necessary for the
maintenance of law and order within our own border. Canada has no need for greater armaments.
For some years past some of us have been maintaining that it was not necessary to have an armed force to repel invasion. We have been inclined to say that the armed force in Canada existed for the sake of keeping down any disorder which might arise within our own borders. When we made that statement it was hotly challenged, and the reply was made that our armed force did not exist for that purpose, but that we had armaments as an insurance against war. Now we find that in the course of a very admirable speech at Geneva, to which I had the privilege of listening, and which created a very good impression, so far as the attitude of Canada toward militarism was concerned, the Minister of Justice, who led the delegation, said very definitely that our naval, military and air forces are no larger than are necessary to keep order within our own borders. I think it is most serious if we have to spend these millions of dollars simply to keep our own Canadians in order. It is most unfortunate if the definite statement has to be made that we have such unrest in Canada that it is necessary to have the warships-which, we have been told by the minister are very efficient- to keep our own people in order.
A few days ago I read in a Vancouver paper that one of our cruisers came from Victoria to the docks at Vancouver in order to be present on May day in case of emergency. To my mind that is a serious reflection upon our country and our administration. The same applies to the army. Some of us have protested against the extension of our mounted police force, because in reality I understand it is a military unit. I think it was the Prime Minister who stated the other day that there was no military drill, no bayonet drill or riot squad drill such as had been described by Regina papers. I am absolutely at a loss to know why such an item should appear in the newspapers, and why there should be put into the mouth of the officer in charge the statement which appeared in the press.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I did not discuss the
Regina situation at all; it was the Ottawa situation I dealt with.
Oh, I understood-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It must have been some other member; it was not I.

I thought the Prime Minister was dealing with the Regina situation.
Supply-National Defence

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, I dealt with the one in Ottawa.

Then I am mistaken in the matter. Someone else made the statement-possibly it was the Minister of Justice -that there was no riot squad or riot drill. I am very glad to team that the Royal Canadian Mounted police are not engaged in bayonet drill. Undoubtedly however we have other forces engaged in bayonet drill, which are ready at any time to repress disorders in Canada. I know it is necessary to maintain peace, order and good government in this country; otherwise civilized life would become impossible. I protest however that this is not the way to bring about peace, order and good government. We have what might be termed a law-abiding people. I cannot very well conceive of an exhibition of greater patience than has been shown by our people during this last year or two in the fane of very great hardships. I think it is an insult to them to have it said at Geneva-although it was said perhaps with the very good purpose of trying to show how small our armament was and how much we were in favour of general world peace-I submit it is no less than an insult to say that we spend millions of dollars a year in order to keep up a force to maintain order in this country. I would urge that instead of these large amounts being spent in this way on military equipment and the maintenance of a military force, we spend a little bit more in helping our people in this time of stress. It is noit merely the labour people whom I have been trying to represent specially in this house, but tens of thousands of other citizens who cannot understand why this government should go on adopting these repressive measures and failing to introduce constructive measures to relieve the prevailing distress. I think I am fair in asking the minister responsible: Was the Minister of Justice correct in stating-perhaps that is an awkward question to put, and I do not intend it in any nasty way-

Even a number of our banks are now feeling the necessity of having trained economists on their staff. Is there any thought at all that the Dominion government will some time have a man regularly equipped for the purpose as adviser to the Finance' deipartment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can only say that from
the knowledge and experience I have acquired in the limited time I have been in the department I think the country is extremely well served in the character and ability of the permanent officials of the Department of Finance with whom I have icome in contact. They are men singularly well informed and unusually devoted to their duties. They are there on all occasions, putting in long hours without reference to either clock or calendar. They are always on service, and I must say that I take delight in this opportunity of paying tribute to the quality of their service and the spirit in which they serve.

What I had in
mind was a little different from what the minister seems to have in his mind. I am not in any way suggesting that the employees of the Finance department are not faithful and capable men. What I do suggest is that we are faced with a very difficult situation to-day. Everyone recognizes that a great many of the older methods of conducting public finance are not altogether suitable to the present needs. Anyone who has kept at all in touch with the. discussions which have been going on in England in the last few years, or with those that have been going on between bankers on the continent or at Geneva, must recognize that a great many governmental people are alive to the need for very close study of the entire economic situation. I take it that the very fact that the men in the department are working long hours and are quite efficient in dealing with the ordinary routine business explains why they are precluded from giving that study which somebody ought to give to the larger economic affairs of the country. My thought was that if even a bank finds it necessary, or at any rate advisable, to have at least one economist on its staff, it might be well that the Finance department of this country should undertake to engage at least one trained economist on its staff who could devote himself to a study of the general economic situation as it exists to-day, and to a study also of some of the proposals which are put forward from time to tame for the improvement of conditions. In this house we have taken up the question of inflation as a possible method of correcting

Supply-Finance
some of the evils with which we are faced at the present time,, and from time to time there has 'been a suggestion that we ought to stabilize our currency. I do not know that we have anyone in the department who is able to devote himself to a study of this kind of thing. If we are to develop into the position where at some time we shall have a central bank, and if we are not only going to carry out a system of rediscounting but going into open market transactions, it seems to me it would be very essential to have somebody who would be able to advise as to possible extensions for modifications of the Finance Act with respect to the best means by which we. could possibly adopt a system of central banking. It is only a year from now until the Bank Act comes up in due course for revision, and I have no doubt a great many proposals will be made then. It seems to me, therefore, that instead of waiting for pressure from outside, it would be a good thing for the department to engage its own experts. If we cannot obtain them in Canada, let us go elsewhere; but I suggest that the department should have experts who would be able to devote special attention to the new needs which are arising at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If we got into the realm
of banking, finance, currency and that sort of thing, it would be difficult for one to place one's finger on any particular individual who would be regarded as expert, to the exclusion of others. As a matter of fact, there are as many different points of view as there are individuals who make a study of the subject. Without minimizing the suggestion offered by my hon. friend, may I say to him that if it transpires, in the judgment of the government, that the staff of the Department of Finance, as it at present exists, requires enlargement, so far as I am concerned, I shall be one of the first to give heed to what he has said.

The minister will
understand, I think, that if there is some difficulty in obtaining from the realm of experts men who would be able to advise, it is much more difficult, surely, for the minister, however capable he may be, to bring to the task that specialized knowledge which I suggest is necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no one more ready than the minister himself to admit very freely his limitation in all the spheres to which the hon. gentleman refers.

I take it we are dealing with item 7 on page 8 of the estimates, which covers salaries and contingencies of the
department of the inspector general of banks. I notice that there is a decrease of 16,600 in this item, and I should like to know how this decrease is made up and just what the duties are of the inspector general of banks and his officials.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would refer my hon. friend to section 56 of the Bank Act, which outlines fully the duties of the inspector general of banks.
That does not give me very much information. Surely the minister can tell me in a few words just what are the duties of this official.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Subsection 8 of section 56 reads as follows:-
The inspector, from time to time, but not less frequently than once in each calendar year, shall make or cause to be made, such examination and inquiry into the affairs or business of each bank as he may deem to be necessary or expedient, and for such purposes take charge of the premises of the assets of the bank or any portion thereof, if the need should arise, for the purpose of satisfying himself that the provisions of this act having reference to the safety of the creditors and shareholders of each bank are being duly observed and that the bank is in a sound financial condition, and at the conclusion of each such examination and inquiry shall report thereon to the minister.
How often are the head offices of the banks visited?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Visits are made as provided for by the act, not less than once a year, but the inspector general keeps in close contact with the banks; the frequency of his visits would be dependent upon the condition prevailing in any particular bank. Some banks might require more careful consideration than others. The frequency of inspection is governed entirely by the circumstances.

During the last
calendar year has the inspector general visited the head offices of all the banks in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
And he has made a report to the Minister of Finance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, he has complied with the act in every particular.

Has the inspector
* general visited the head offices of the banks of Canada more than once during the last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is a question which I cannot answer offhand with any accuracy. I think I can safely say that the inspector general

has visited the head offices of the banks in his inspectorial capacity to the fullest extent as required by the act. I know he is keeping in very close touch with the situation with respect to every one of the chartered banks of Canada.
I take it that the Minister of Finance during the short time he has been in office is satisfied with the inspection made by this official and his staff?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My answer would be in the affirmative, with the reservation that it is based upon the knowledge I have been able to glean during the limited time I have been at the head of the department. I do not wish my latter statement to minimize in the slightest my fullest confidence in the character of the inspection and of the inspector general himself.
I may say I am entirely satisfied with the answer of the minister, but he has not answered my question as to how the reduction in the item is made up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The major portion of the reduction is due to salary deduction, and partly to the fact that an over-estimation had been made of the expenses normally required.
Is the major portion due to the ten per cent cut?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In round figures, the amount of the salary deduction is $1,600, and the balance is made up by an over-estimation of the expenses required for the office.

The difference between $6,600, the amount of the reduction, and $1,600, the amount of the ten per cent cut, is $5,000. My only object in drawing this matter to the attention of the committee is to point out that in this time of stress and strain the morale of the people would not be helped by a reduction in the staff of this department. I am quite sure the committee would be willing that this staff should be maintained, or increased if necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am quite in accord with the views expressed by the hon. member for South Perth. I think this department should be the last place in which to practise economy, if to do so would mean an impairment of its efficiency. However, I may say to my hon. friend that we have been governed entirely by the judgment of the inspector general, and I am satisfied that there will be no impairment of efficiency.
Why has the interest rate on currency issued to banks been reduced' from four and a half per cent to three per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It -was reduced for a time, but it has since been increased. The reduction was made for several reasons, one being to conform to the discount rate in force in London and New York. The reduction had a more particular reference to the fact that at the time of the launching of the national service loan we wanted to make it as easy as possible for the banks to accommodate customers who were subscribers to the loan.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Miscellaneous-grant to the Montreal Association for the Blind, $4,500.

I do not want to object to the grant in this case, but I should like to urge upon the minister that the government take some definite action with regard to providing more adequately for the blind. This is for one group. I am thinking of the larger problem which we have in Canada. The blind have petitioned again and again that they be given some sort of pension; that their special disability be recognized and that they be put on a basis where they can depend upon drawing a regular amount. I believe Manitoba has agreed to assume its share if pensions for the blind are put upon the same basis as old age pensions, and it would seem reasonable there should be an extension along this line. We have recognized in the case of the burnt-out men that they had special claims and I think, on the whole, there is no other class of people who receive greater sympathy from the public generally than the blind who are so helpless.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sure we all feel sympathetic towards the blind, and I know there is not a single hon. member who would not wish to lean backward in his endeavour to make their lot easier in this life, if that were possible. So far we have been dealing with old age pensions in agreement with the provinces. I hope the time is not far removed when we shall be able to take on the burden entirely as a federal matter, and at that time, or before if the opportunity should present itself, I may say I shall be glad to give sympathetic consideration to the suggestion made by my hon. friend.

Would the minister explain the amount that is asked for under this appropriation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member will recall that we have introduced a new practice and that now we have a comptroller of the treasury. The new Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act provides, amongst other things, a system of centralized expenditure and commitment control under the jurisdiction of the comptroller of the treasury. This act came into force on April 1 last, and now all expenses in accounting offices are accountable to the comptroller of the treasury.
Does this mean an increase in the accounting work, or is it offset by a saving?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot give my hon. friend the exact figures, but I am satisfied that the work of the comptroller of the treasury will, in the course of a year, save two or three times over the total cost of the vote for his office, not only in efficiency and more accurate control, but in various other ways. This new system will be very much to the advantage of the public treasury.
Is it the intention to move all the accounting officials from the various departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They have all been transferred and are under the control of the Department of Finance.

Have they
actually been taken out of the various departments and placed under the comptroller of the treasury?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Is the intention to have that done?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As the circumstances require. They are all under the comptroller of the treasury, although many of them are, for the time being, remaining in their several departments; but the organization itself is now centralized directly under the comptroller of the treasury.
I suppose the fact that all the accounting is centralized will facilitate answers to questions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think, on the whole, we have shown remarkable efficiency in answering questions and responding to returns this year.	.
Yes, especially this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the history of parliament, there has been nothing comparable in number and volume with the answers and returns which have been required in the last two years, and I may say that the hon. member for Temiscouata has not been over-modest in this regard.
Are we to understand that this appropriation is largely to pay salaries under the comptroller of the treasury?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Largely for salaries. For
example, last year we had in the main estimates an item amounting to $80,000 for unforeseen expenses; in the supplementary estimates, an item of $25,000 for administration of the Consolidated Revenue Act, and another item of S25,000, unforeseen expenses, further amount required. I am heartily in sympathy with the move, but is it not a fact that there is still a number of accountancy officers in various departments and paid out of the civil government votes for those departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As I informed my hon. friend a moment ago, many of these officers are physically in the several departments, although they are now under the control of the comptroller of the treasury. Many of them will be paid from the civil government votes for the several departments this year, but at the end of this fiscal year all these civil votes will appear under the vote for the comptroller of the treasury.

That is just the information I was seeking. I was under the impression that a large number of these officers were still paid out of the civil government votes of the several departments in which they are stationed. But after this year all these officers will be paid out of this vote?

I should like to put two or three questions to the minister with reference to the national service loan. Was it sold to investment houses, and if so, at what price? What commission was given to them for handling it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The national service loan was handled by a voluntary committee located in Montreal, under the Chairmanship of Sir Charles Gordon, president of the Bank of Montreal. Their services were entirely

voluntary and no salaries were paid, mot even expenses for that matter. The loan was sold only to the individual subscribers. There was no sale other than to those who purchased the bonds.

question to answer in specific terms. I am exceedingly anxious, however, that the board be set up at an early date.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is nothing left for it to do now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh yes, there is.

I can see
no need for the board, especially in view of the system of the present government in regard to tariffs. They make tariffs overnight, and no tariff board is necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should think my hon.
friends would be most anxious to have the board set up, so that it may help them to steady the government, and prevent it from doing any more mischief.
I should be only too glad to have it, if that end could be accomplished.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I understand
the board has power to deal with only such matters as the government may refer to it. That is my recollection of the legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot say, offhand.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I believe the
minister will find that to be correct.

Will the government make
use of the tariff board before bringing down any further increases in the tariff?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should not like to commit the government categorically to an undertaking of that character. I am sure the government will utilize the services of the board to the fullest possible extent, compatible with public service.

I am wondering if the ten
per cent reduction will apply to the salaries of the tariff board appointees?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have
not any salaries with which to deal, so far. I do not wish to argue upon hypothetical questions, because I find it difficult enough to answer the real ones.

Is there any

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot give
my hon. friend an accurate answer.
All right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that the vote which was provided by parliament last year, following the disastrous fire, was very substantial. Speaking from memory my impression is that a great part of that vote is still unused. At the moment I know of no application from the harbour board which has not been dealt with. There are deficits
resulting from the operation of the Montreal harbour bridge. We have known of the enormous amounts that the bridge has cost, over and above the original estimate. I think it is common knowledge that things are in a very unsatisfactory condition generally. I should like to ask the minister if the government has considered the desirability of having some sort of commission or committee investigate this whole affair before continuing to loan large sums of money to the Montreal harbour commissioners. I do not wish more boards of inquiry travelling around the country than are necessary, but this is a matter which ought to be straightened out, and it might very well have been done at this session. I would urge that the minister take into consideration the necessity of cleaning up the whole matter and letting the public know at least something about where their money has gone in the last few years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The question whether or
not there ought to be a royal commission of investigation into the affairs of the Montreal harbour bridge is one entirely apart from the question whether or not we should meet our statutory obligations. In conjunction with the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal in proportion to their share of commitments, we must comply with the act of parliament providing for any deficiences which may arise between receipts and expendi-tureSj as a result of the guarantee of securities in respect of that undertaking. fMr. Rhodes.]
Quebec and the city of Montreal. The direct question whether there will or will not be a commission of inquiry is one which at the moment I am not in a position to answer.

Would the minister be
good enough to give the information as to the various items which go to make up this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Certainly. This appropriation is for the amount which it is estimated the revenue of the Montreal harbour bridge will fall short of the interest payable up to and including November 1, 1932. As my hon. friend knows that is on an issue of some $19,000,000 of harbour commissioners' bonds guaranteed by the dominion, and issued for the capital cost of the bridge. The estimate is made up as follows:	The annual interest
on $19,000,000 dominion guaranteed five per cent bonds is $950,000, less current cash, $18,600. Surplus, operating revenues over operating expenses, $245,400; contributions from province and city under agreement, $300,000, making a total of $564,000, which deducted from the sum first mentioned leaves $386,000. Then we must add the estimated cost of exchange on the $950,000 interest payable in New York. This estimate has been made up on a fifteen per cent basis. This of course can be only a computation. We cannot tell from day to day or week to week what the premium may be upon funds in New York.

How much
will it amount to?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will be $142,500, but to the extent that is enlarged or diminished, to that extent will it be greater or smaller.
So if exchange were at par you would actually have a deduction of about $145,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; at par the figure would be $386,000.
Does that mean the bridge at the moment falls short of earning operating expenses and interest to the extent of nearly $900,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. The operating revenue over operating expenses is $245,400. If the hon. gentleman will subtract that figure he will get the deficit, because, as he has recalled, $300,000 of this is made up of contributions by the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal by virtue of their guarantees..

Then the
deficit is between $600,000 and $700,000, with the city and the' province contributing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In round figures.
So far as the actual deficit after applying the surplus over operation and maintenance is concerned, you say it is $900,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have just told my hon. friend that the fixed charges amount to $950,-
000.	That is not taking into consideration the question of premium upon American funds. The actual operating revenue in excess of operating expenses at the moment is $245,400. If he will just subtract one from the other he will find the answer to his question.
How much of this $300,000 are the province and the city contributing; and what is the amount of their respective guarantees?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The province of Quebec
and the city of Montreal are each obligated to the extent of payment of interest amounting to $150,000 a year. The guarantee of the dominion is for the excess.
Is all the amount asked for here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As the Prime Minister points out, we cannot escape our guarantee. In other words, if the province and the city fail to implement their respective guarantees, we would be obligated for the whole; but inasmuch as the province and the city are meeting their obligations, we pay the excess.
Is it expected to take $528,000 to pay our share of the guarantee?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Our share of the guarantee at the moment, according to our estimate, is $386,000, but the excess making the figure 8528,000 arises out of the premium on New York funds. That is all over and above the amount of the guarantees provided by the province and the city.
What are the respective contributions by the province, the city and the dominion? And what will be the percentage of any losses to be borne by them respectively?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under the agreement entered into by the commissioners with the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal, the province and the city have each agreed to pay one-third of the annual deficit up to $450,000 for forty years; that is a maximum of 8300,000 a year.
If the deficit was greater than $300,000 they would not pay more -than one-third of their maximum commitment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Quite so.
What was the estimated cost in the first place, and what the actual capital cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The capital cost of the
bridge to December 31st, 1931, was $18,639,263. I do not know what figure was stated as being the estimated cost so far as this parliament is concerned, because I was not here and have not refreshed my mind on the point. However, I find that in the preamble of the legislation passed by the Quebec legislature in 1926, in virtue of which the province gave its guarantee, the estimated cost of construction was given as $10,000,000.
What is the exact amount of the bonds outstanding on account of this bridge; is it the same as the capital cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: And the rate of interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Five per cent, payable half yearly.
Were the bonds sold at par?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not that information before me, but I am advised that not only did they sell at par; a portion of the last issue sold at a small premium.
What was the total contribution by the dominion to the cost of the bridge?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no contribution
at all towards the cost of the bridge, only the guarantee. Has my hon. friend in mind how much money we have paid in virtue of our guarantee?
What is the total amount that we will be obligated for by virtue of our guarantee?	-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are obligated upon the whole issue of $19,000,000.

What is the total for
the guarantees by the province and the city?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The city of Montreal and the province of Quebec have agreed to guarantee the interest so far as there may be a deficit in earnings to the maximum amount of $300,000 per year.

Some weeks ago I put
certain questions on the order paper, and these were passed as orders for returns. I do not wish to ask the minister to hold this item up until such time as that information is tabled, but I should like to get it at the earliest pos-

sible date. I would support the suggestion of the member for Winnipeg North Centre that a very thorough investigation be made into the whole question of this excess expenditure. I think this information is due to the house and to the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The delay in responding
to the orders for returns is due entirely to the circumstance that we are dependent upon the harbour commissioners of Montreal, from whom we must expect the information to be able to give a satisfactory response to the motion made by my hon. friend.
