Who audits the accounts of the harbour commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The books of the Montreal harbour commission are audited by their own auditors. Of course, we have a right to send in our auditors to check up the accounts of the commission.

When the legislation
dealing with the Montreal and other harbour commissioners was being put through the former Minister of Finance informed the house that the audit board had jurisdiction to audit their accounts. Has the board made any investigation into the accounts of the Montreal harbour commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am informed that the
board, some two years ago. made an andit of the accounts of the Montreal harbour commission at the instance of the then Minister of Finance. So far as I know, there has been no government audit since that time. I may add that an audit has since been made by Price, Waterhouse & Company.

Is any information
available to the house regarding the results of any audit, either by the audit board or by Price, Waterhouse & Company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not personally familiar with the matter to the extent of being able to give my hon. friend information of my own knowledge, but as I understand it, the audit of Price. Waterhouse & Company disclosed that the accounts were in order. There are audits and audits, but so far as the ac-

counts themselves were concerned, the audit in question disclosed that they were in order I have no doubt that a copy of the report could be obtained for the hon. gentleman.
Is that all the information the minister can give-that the accounts were in order?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is all I can give at
the moment, because I have not seen either the accounts or the report itself.
Has it ever been determined why there was such a tremendous increase in the cost of the bridge in comparison with the estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no knowledge of
the matter, either officially or personally. It has been intimated to me that the bridge was made considerably heavier and the amount of metal that went into it was greater than contemplated when the original estimates were prepared. I only pass on that limited amount of information for what it is worth.
What is the attitude of the government towards this question? Has the government made a real effort to discover why the bridge cost so much more than was originally expected?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I was Minister of Finance during the period to which the hon. gentleman refers. Price, Waterhouse & Company were asked to make a report, which they did, and it indicates that from the books of the commission it was apparent that the vouchers were there for the expenditures that had been made, not in detail, but for the purpose of enabling them to certify that sums had been expended as received. That is as far as it went. As to why the structure cost the additional sum beyond the original estimate, there is no definite information before this house, and, frankly, I can see great difficulties in obtaining it in detail. It is not difficult to obtain this information, for instance, that the inspection cost several hundred thousand dollars. One of the inspectors was a gentleman who resided in Chicago and who visited the property twice; the voucher was there for the money he received. That is what I mean when I say that the report was vindicated.

I have this last question. Will the government make an effort to inquire into this matter?-because it is really a question that should be looked into, and the reasons should be made known if reasons can be found.

Supply-Finance

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: With respect to that, two gentlemen who could -contribute largely to information in that regard are dead, if not a third. That fact has been apparent for some time. There is, however, shall I say, a possibility of information being obtained as to why, in one branch of the work, so much more money was spent than anticipated. But even in that regard I cannot speak with any degree of certainty. I received the report-I was in the Finance department-and it is in the hands of the Marine department, to which it is addressed, the Minister of Marine being the minister responsible for the commission. But nothing short of -an inquiry that goes far beyond the question of the mere production of vouchers for debits and credits would in any sense answer the question asked by the hon. gentleman, and certainly it is not a matter that -could be easily answered affirmatively or negatively at the present time.

I do not like to press the question I asked a little while ago, before -the Prime Minister -came in, but I do urge that in view of the tremendous amounts involved and the heavy burden on the people of Canada, we have some right to have a further inquiry into this matter. I -cannot quite think that in a matter of this kind our knowledge must be entirely dependent upon one or two men who may be dead. It seems to me that if a proper inquiry were instituted, information could be obtained. Rather than the Dominion government and the people of Canada having to -carry this enormous burden, which apparently we shall have to shoulder from now on, it seems to me that we have a right -to have the situation cleared up. I would point out to the Prime Minister that there is a good deal of feeling throughout the country with regard to this matter, and since there have been a large number of -other investigations, it is considered very generally that this matter ought to be investigated. The present government is in -a good position to carry out the investigation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Possibly the hon. gentleman would say that I would not be loath to conduct an investigation. But one does not desire to conduct investigations merely for the purpose of mud-slinging if it serves no useful -public purpose. Now this is the fact. The Dominion has guaranteed interest on $19,000,000 worth of bonds and payment of their principal, and these securities are held largely in the United States of America. The coupons are presented in New York every six months for payment. Practically the whole of them come in, as the hon. gentleman can readily understand, through New York offices, the 11761-187
principal -and interest -being both payable in United States funds. Whether we like it or not, that interest must -be met every six months, because a default in that regard is a default of this country whose guarantee is endorsed upon the coupons of the -bonds. The operating revenue of -the bridge should increase with the increasing growth of Montreal, and it is also not improbable that by reason -of the provision for a tramway to cross th-e bridge there will be some added revenue. At the present moment a bus service operates on the bridge and it is intended -to extend the tramway. As I understand it, that is the position at the moment.
The explanation given for the increased cost is twofold. First, the acquisition of large blocks of real estate for the approaches to the structure was made at a greater cost than was anticipated and, second, it was necessary to use heavier steel than was anticipated. I understand that the weight -of metal absorbed in the construction of this bridge was several hundred tons more than was originally estimated.
Hundreds of thousands.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I understood it was
hundreds of thousands of pounds or thousands of tons. The costs of fabrication, of inspection and legal expenses were -much greater than was at first expected.
If my memory serves me correctly, the last bonds were not sold until 1930, and the price obtained was over par; they had been deposited as security and then they were sold with the guarantee of this country at a time when bonds were commanding very excellent prices. I say frankly to the hon. gentleman that if, as and when there is any likelihood of the exact .causes of the greatly increased price becoming known by any reasonable investigation, that investigation will be made. However, it must be realized that this is a most difficult thing to do, especially when there are produced vouchers for weights of metal and explanations are forthcoming as to why the cost per pound was greater than anticipated. A special make of steel was needed in the construction of -the heavy members of the bridge. All this information is contained in the report made by Price, Waterhouse & Company, who stated that beyond that they, as auditors, could not go.

Has -the minister an auditor's statement to show that this i-s the correct amount of the deficit on the operation of the bridge and, if so, who were the auditors?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry I have not that information a,t hand, but I shall be glad to obtain it for my hon. friend.

Does not the minister think that he should have an auditor's statement before he advances this money? We should be sure that we are not paying any more than we are called upon to pay by the terms of the guarantee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree that it is incumbent upon the Department of Finance to make sure that the accounts are correct before payment is made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I may say to the hon.
member for Macleod that when payments are made the coupons are actually taken over by the government to form part of the assets which we hold for some future occasion, they constitute a charge against the undertaking.
The point I was presenting to the minister was that we should ascertain the actual deficit on the bridge.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is done by the harbour commission.

If I remember correctly, an estimate was made of the expected traffic across the bridge, and it strikes me that $245,000 is not much below what should be expected at this stage in the history of the structure. If I remember correctly the estimate for 1932 was $500,000, and that was why the city of Montreal and the province of Quebec came forward with their guarantees.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The estimate made before construction was that the annual revenue from the bridge would be 1250,000.
That was for the first year, but it should increase.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That called for a contri-oution from the city of Montreal of $116,666, and a like contribution from the province of Quebec and from the commission itself. As my hon. friend knows, the commission has not been able to implement its guarantee.
It is only natural that there should be a considerable diminution in the traffic, as there has been in all projects of this character.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The approaches to the bridge on the other side of the river from Montreal are a provincial work. Their construction has been delayed in such a manner that the traffic which ordinarily would be expected to use the bridge has not found it convenient to do so.
Mr. STEWART 'Edmonton): That was my information.
[Mr. Coote.J

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no information before me which would answer the question asked by the hon. member for West Edmonton.

If I remember correctly, it was expected that in 1932 the bridge would earn something like $500,000 in tolls. Last year it earned $245,000 but, as my hon. friend has pointed out, more traffic would have used the bridge had it been in position to receive it.

I do not think the figures given by the minister are quite satisfactory to the committee. When the Prime Minister was leader of the opposition I remember his drawing the attention of the house to the vast amount of money spent on this bridge. I understand the first estimate was that it would cost some $6,000,000, and the amount eventually rose to $19,000,000. When the Prime Minister first took over his present office he again drew the attention of the house to this extraordinary expenditure, and I was in hopes that an investigation of some sort would be made into this matter. It seems to me that the reasons given for not holding an investigation are not as satisfactory as they should be. It has been said that three men who might have given some information with regard to this bridge have died, but that does not seem to me to be a good reason why we should not be able to find out where this great expenditure has gone. The Department of Finance has the right to send in auditors to check up, and this information should be available for the benefit of the committee. The Prime Minister has said that a special steel was needed for this bridge, but surely any engineer capable of being put in charge of a huge undertaking like this should have known the kind of steel that would be required, before the first estimates were made. Such an engineer might have been forgiven for being out a million or two, but there is no excuse for an increase from $6,000,000 to $19,000,000. Even if everything is above board, surely those who have made such huge mistakes and have cost the country so much should be penalized for their bad judgment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I omitted to mention that a considerable sum was absorbed in interest during construction. Shortly after this government came into power we asked Price, Waterhouse & Company to make a report. I think it is in the office of the Minister of Marine. I believe we can get it and lay it on the table. It will show anyway how the sum of $19,000,000 was reached.

Supply-Finance

No doubt the Prime
Minister has looked over that report. I should like to ask him if, in the light of his own great ability, he is satisfied, from reading the report, with the way in which the money was spent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
Is the Prime Minister
satisfied to let the matter rest there, or does he intend to try to find out more?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He has already said what he is trying to do.
In the $19,000,000, what was the relative amount spent on real estate and that spent on the bridge itself? Was the contract let on the cost plus basis of the construction?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As to the first question.
I would not trust my memory to give the answer. The document which I shall endeavour to have brought down will give that.

Can the right hon.
gentleman give the approximate cost?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not care to trust
my memory. The auditors' report will show exactly what was spent for real estate and the cost of the bridge. On the second point, the commissioners themselves acquired the real estate, but they let a contract for the construction of the metal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have the details covering some thirty or more items which go to make up the cost of $18,639,000. I do not know whether the committee desires that I should read them or not, but if necessary I shall do so.

What we are entitled to is an idea of the original estimate, the cost of the real estate and of the building of the bridge. Then we would be able to compare that 'with the amount expended on real estate and on the bridge in the $19,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As I have already stated, I have no record of the original estimate. The figure named in the preamble to the Quebec act was $10,000,000. What the figure was which was stated in the house, I cannot say.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hansard says $6,000,000.

The sum
of $6,000,000 was not the estimated cost of the bridge, but the amount which the government was committed to originally in the guarantee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Meighen asked how
much the bridge would cost, and the hon. member for Richelieu said "six million."

I do not
know how he could have mentioned that amount. There is no need to send for Hansard. There is no doubt that the bridge was to cost $10,000,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I know something about the bridge. As a representative of a Montreal constituency, I have taken considerable interest in the matter. The bridge as constructed is entirely different, so far as its proportions, supports and expenditures are concerned, from the one originally contemplated.
The pillars upon which the bridge rests are very much larger and more expensive, and the steel in it runs to hundreds, even thousands of tons more than originally planned. I have been told that the cost of the steel alone was between $2,000,000 and $3,000,000 beyond what was first contemplated. I took the trouble to ask the auditors-I suppose I had no right to do so-with regard to the audit and they said that there was not a single expenditure for which the voucher was missing in the audit. Every voucher was there, showing in the aggregate the cost of the bridge as reported. If you wish an investigation, it is not one by auditors, because everything is in order to satisfy the most careful audit possible. The question is whether some of those expenditures in connection with real estate and otherwise, were simulated or not, if I may use that term, but I have made personal inquiry, not as a member of government, and I have not so far found the slightest fact which would indicate that such is the case.

The statement of the Secretary of State opens up a new question altogether in so far as this bridge is concerned. His statement is to the effect that the present bridge is not to be compared with what was estimated when the legislation passed this house. He states that the piers upon which the bridge is built are much heavier and more expensive than was contemplated when the legislation passed the House of Commons and the agreement was entered into. He also states that the steel in the bridge is much greater in tonnage than the estimate. It

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It is perfectly obvious that the harbour commissioners of Montreal were responsible, subject to the oversight, such as it was, of the then Minister of Marine.
Did they get the consent of the then Minister of Marine?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not know the secrets of the former government, but in any case, I have no access now to the approvals given by the former Minister of Marine. But the cost of that bridge is fully vouched for. I am giving the best information I can obtain, although it is not official. I am speaking as a member of this house; as Secretary of State I have nothing to do with the bridge or the expenditures on it; but as a representative of a Montreal division, I am interested in the matter. I have made inquiries and I have no doubt that the entire expenditure is properly vouched for. Further, it is undoubted that more stable and expensive abutments than originally contemplated were put into the bridge. I am also quite satisfied every bit of that expenditure was approved by the harbour commissioners of Montreal. I would infer that the larger expenditures, when contemplated, were approved in due course by the then Minister of Marine having oversight and supervision of that.

Has the Secretary of
State looked up the legislation which gave the harbour commission permission to build this bridge, to find out whether the then Minister of Marine had the right to increase the expenditure over the estimate to the extent done without coming to parliament? Has the Secretary of State any information in that regard?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: At one time I was familiar with that legislation, but I have not looked into it recently and I will not trust to memory for the purpose of discussing it to-night.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Chapter 58 of the statutes of 1924 cover the point which the hon. gentleman is raising. Section 1 reads:

Mr. Chairman, just before the committee took recess I was making a few remarks upon this item. It seems unfortunate that the only place in which we can discuss a great many of the more important policies of the government is in connection with some one item of this character. Now that the disarmament conference is at work in Geneva and we have subscribed to the Kellogg pact for the renunciation of war as an instrument of policy, it is high time we should reconsider the whole military policy of this country. It is unfortunate that from year to year we take it for granted that we are to go on in the same old way.
I know that on various, occasions there have been expressions of opinion that we desire the world should disarm, that all the other nations should disarm, and yet we ourselves are taking no steps along this line.

There are no steps
to take.

One hon. gentleman suggests there are no steps to take. So long as we have items of this character there are certain steps we can take. We in Canada are in a peculiarly favourable position to carry forward a further measure of disarmament. We have confessedly no foes immediately at our gates. As far as we can see we stand in no danger of invasion. We have been told again and again that we have nothing to fear from the east or west, from the south or north. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), whom I quoted this afternoon, took that attitude at Geneva, where he went so far as to say that the only force we have to-day is that made necessary to maintain law and order in this country. I suggested this afternoon that we were in a very desperate situation if we had to spend somewhere between $10,000,000 and $20,000,000 to maintain law and order in this country. Some time this evening I should like to find out whether the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sutherland) agrees with the Minister of Justice in this regard, whether he thinks in reality our whole military force exists solely for the purpose of maintaining law and order. I do not think he will agree with that. Then we fall back on the other plea, that we need this military force as insurance against war. It is that point which I wish to discuss for a few minutes.
While we complain of other countries being rather hypocritical in this regard, we should remember that we have certain responsibilities ourselves. Some time ago I came across in the New Leader of April 18, 1930, a fable, a sort of satire dealing with the naval conference.. I will read it because I think it applies equally to the disarmament conference which is in session at the present time:
The Lion, the Eagle, the Tiger, the Crocodile and the Shark, met in conference to consider the advisability of holding preliminary conver-
Supply-National Defence

sations with a view to preparing the way for a meeting to consider the possibility of holding a conference to discuss the project of an eventual attempt to effect some limitation of teeth and claws.
The audience consisted of a Bear (who appeared to be amused) and, at some distance, a Deer and two Rabbits.
The Lion, who presided, was looking even more saintly than usual, for he had constructed a tin halo for himself which would have been still more impressive if the Tiger had not unfortunately licked off most of the gilt. On the halo were written the words, "My Glorious Mission."
The president opened the proceedings by saying that as there had been a great demand among the weaker animals for teeth control and the limitation of claws, it had been thought well to hold a conference to talk about these things.
The main thing was to talk, and for his own part he loved to hear his own voice, but he did not intend to have his own teeth taken out because he had always used his teeth and claws for the benefit of others, and never for his own advantage. Teeth and claws were essential to the existence of lions, they were not superfluities, in fact, he said, "Teeth is us." He realized also that in some degree this was true of all present. At this point the Crocodile shed several large tears.
The Lion, continuing, said that he thought they might all agree to the abolition of fins and propellers which served no good purpose. To this the Tiger and the Eagle signified assent, but the Shark and the Crocodile showed their teeth, the Shark observing that the prohibition of claws and wings would be more to the general good.
The Eagle said he was all for prohibition, but of teeth rather than olaws. He had been accused of devouring hares (the Rabbits disappeared at this juncture), but he could truly say that his action had always been for the uplift of these earth-bound creatures.
The Tiger observed that some people were rather too uplifted for his taste, and he agreed with the Shark that wings should be forbidden. He was tired of flap-doodle.
At this moment the Lion uttered a low growl, because the Eagle was twisting his tail, while the Tiger took opportunity to pull out some of the Eagle's feathers, and received in return such a peck on the ear as caused him to retreat hastily. Meanwhile the Shark bit off the end of the Crocodile's tail, and was rewarded with a scratch that turned the water red.
The meeting then broke up, and the following official statement was handed to the Press:-
"Our conference has been a striking success, complete agreement has been reached on all points, and the utmost cordiality has prevailed throughout."
That satire is only too true of past disarmament conferences, and from all that we can judge at this distance that depicts what is going on at the present time at Geneva. It does not seem fair that we should blame everyone else for the delay in disarmament.
I can very well understand how France might fear to disarm; I can understand her fear of a war of revenge. I can understand her sense

of a lack of security and all that kind of thing. I can understand how Germany feels at the present time, disarmed as she has been, yet with the other nations not having carried out their part of the contract. I can understand how through central Europe each nation is afraid to take the lead in disarmament. But in this country it does seem to me, although we are a very small nation, small in population and perhaps in influence, that it might be possible for us at least to make a gesture that would have considerable effect in Europe. Instead of simply going along year after year in the same direction we pursued before the war, and which the war proved did not provide anything like real security, we in Canada, in view of the whole world situation, might very well take some lead in a forward movement.
May I foe permitted to refer to-night to a very excellent article that appeared in MacLean's Magazine of August 1, 1931. It is headed "Salesmen of Death. The Truth about War Makers" by Lieutenant-Colonel George A. Drew. I wish to quote from this article because, though there may be nothing particularly new in it, it is provocative .of thought and should be widely read. In fact, in many respects the general public outside, with regard to matters of this kind, is in advance of the opinion, if we have any, which exists in this house; at least it is less apathetic than parliament regarding such matters. Colonel Drew sums up in one or two paragraphs his views:
One serious obstacle that must be overcome in convincing the people of the world that disarmament is everybody's business is the cynical attitude which is all too common that war is an inevitable evil and that the most we can do is to postpone it as long as possible and, when the time does come, hope to be just a little better armed than our enemy. Hand in hand with this attitude is the belief that we maintain peace by being better armed than our neighbour and thus preventing attack. An excellent example of this point of view is furnished in the following extract from an editorial in the Canadian Defence Quarterly of April 1931:
"The world to-day has prohibited aggressive warfare but defensive wars are permitted; therefore, the nations still regard the use of armaments as the ultimate instrument of national security. So long as this condition remains, human nature decrees that each nation will strive to be armed with armament superior in quality, and if possible quantity, to that of other nations. It is doubtful, therefore, if nations would forego the abundant benefits which result from private enterprise in the armament field."
Words like these have been repeated so often that they have acquired general acceptance without any appreciation of their full import. No one, yet, has been able to demonstrate the "abundant benefits" resulting from private enterprise in the armament field, unless they be the enormous increase in the casualties to all

Supply-National Defence
combatants, or the huge profits acquired by men like Zaharoff, Krupp, Schneider and Grace. . . . That these words appeared in so responsible a journal as the Canadian Defence Quarterly such a comparatively short time before the World Disarmament Conference emphasizes the fact that much remains to be done if the Canadian delegates are to have behind them a well-informed Canadian public opinion. . . . There is ample reason for demanding, as a first step, the elimination of "Propagandists of Hate" by a mutual agreement, effective throughout the world, dissolving the vicious alliance between armament production and profit-sharing corporate enterprise.
It seems to me that instead of going through these estimates as a matter of form, instead of following the old policy of keeping up a skeleton organization which may be expanded at any time for either defensive or aggressive purposes, we should devote ourselves definitely to eliminating the causes of war. Perhaps the Minister of National Defence will say that that is not his job; I can quite understand his taking that attitude, yet his predecessor said on one occasion that he considered himself not as a minister of war but as a minister of peace. If peace is our ideal, if we have renounced war as an instrument of national policy, the responsibility would seem to rest upon someone to do something to promote peace. I have referred to this article by Colonel Drew in which he mentions the enormous fortunes which have been made out of armaments. I do not know whether there are in Canada any armament firms shipping out armaments, but I do not think there are. The Prime Minister nods his head, and I am delighted that we are in that position.

It is very interesting to hear the minister repudiate the statement of the Minister of Justice, but it is unfortunate that the Minister of Justice should have made this statement in such a magnificent assembly as the League of Nations. It is unfortunate, too, that it should have been given as the position of Canada,. when, after all, it was only a general remark called forth doubtless by the peaceful atmosphere which prevailed in that assembly. I am glad to note that there has been some reduction, but I assume that is because of the general policy of economy rather than any desire on the part of the minister to have his military estimates reduced. As we are not preparing against any

one particular enemy, do I understand that the minister is still going on the assumption that armaments are more or less an insurance against war?

speechtext: Yes, absolutely; I think they are an insurance against war.

I am glad to have that statement; it is at least frank. I would point out that the last war did not indicate in any way that the very fullest armaments would prevent a country from being involved. I would point out also that this idea that armaments are insurance against war is out of keeping with the whole conception of the League of Nations. I should like, if I might, to ask the minister whether he thinks, now that we have declared we are renouncing war as an instrument of national policy, there should be any modification in our military policy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The hon. gentleman seems to lose sight of the fact that we are a small nation of ten million people and that we cannot control world policies. We are part of the world, and as long as practically every other nation maintains an army and is not satisfied that conditions are such as to warrant their doing away with it, we cannot do away with ours. It would be just as logical, say, for the city of Toronto to do away entirely with its police force while Detroit, Montreal, Buffalo and all the other large cities were maintaining theirs. There would simply be chaos; all the trouble would be concentrated in Toronto. As long as all other nations have armies, we must continue to have at least the nucleus of one.

The minister would not contend that an army is simply a police force. I take it that in the past armies were maintained in order that a nation might by means of force settle accounts with other nations.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They are to maintain order, the same as a police force. A police force has its prescribed scope of activity in maintaining order. Armies are to maintain international order.
What was the largest amount that was spent on national defence? I understand about five or six years ago it was $20,000,000, was it not?

To that extent I would congratulate the Minister of Defence on having made the reduction. We have a very valuable member in the hon. member for

Winnipeg North Centre, and on many occasions he has rendered' this country useful service, but it seems to me, in view of the fact that these estimates have been so substantially reduced, that in making the argument he has presented this evening he is much like the man who drives a tack with a sledge hammer. It is not so long since I came back from Europe and I heard the hon. gentleman say something about promoting peace. The best way, so far as we are concerned, to promote peace, is to send delegates from this dominion to all the conferences held overseas and to tell the other delegates what a wonderful country we have. On one occasion I had an opportunity of speaking about the 4,000 miles boundary between Canada and the United States and of informing them that we had hardly a single soldier defending it. I am not averse to spending a certain amount of money on an army; we must maintain some sort of army commensurate with the importance of this country, and as I have already said, the minister is to be congratulated upon progressively making so many reductions in his estimates.
Not long ago we had a conference at Bucharest, at which we took up the question of disarmament. The question of an international force for the League of Nations was raised and as the Canadian delegate there I voted against this armed force for the League of Nations, because I thought it was a contradiction of the Kellogg peace pact which practically all the nations in the world had signed. I think we can do the cause of peace a great service if we send our quota of Canadian delegates to all the conferences overseas in order to point out the folly of increasing their armaments. There is no doubt in my mind that on the European continent they are substantially increasing their armaments. We in Canada, on the other hand, are decreasing ours, and that is a fact which the people on the other side of the ocean should take into consideration when such an important question as a policy of peace is being discussed.

I do not want to
prolong this discussion. I have already said that I am glad our armament is small and that there are decreases this year, but I still think that we ought to assume our share of responsibility in regard to general disarmament. As long as we, in the happy position in which we are, practically free from enemies, find it necessary to maintain even a small army, and as long as we uphold the doctrine that armaments are an insurance against war, I do not think we are doing what we might in promoting world peace.

In reference to the skit
which the hon. member read at the beginning of his speech, where the animals could not agree to disarm, what would have happened if, let us say, at that conference the eagle had consented to part with his beak, wings and claws and the others had not?

I do not think that point can be pressed. But of one thing we are sure: as long as we are at the present game we are getting no further ahead. I am inclined to think we are gradually climbing out of the slime. There is no doubt the human race came up through a very bloody pathway, but I am glad to think we are gradually attaining some slight degree of reason in our dealings with one another, and one of these days we shall manage to get along without the teeth and claws.
Is the hon. member suggesting that he is willing that we should completely disarm?
I am.
Forthwith?

Yes, forthwith, so
far as I am concerned, for two reasons. This small army, if you like to call it such, that we are keeping up, is a mere irritant; it is provoking rather than helping to avoid war. More than that, our army is anything but efficient. I should like, if I might, to quote in this connection just one paragraph from a recent address by Sir Arthur Currie. I am not suggesting that he takes the position that I do, but I quote this paragraph from a recent speech of his. He refers to the ghastly toll of past wars. He says:
Some 11,000,000 dead; 9,000,000 war orphans; 5,000,000 war widows; 20,000,000 helpless, wounded, broken men; and 50,000,000 starving unemployed. In the background of this picture were ruins of churches, buildings and humane institutions which had been constructed by the toil and sacrifice of centuries.
Then he declares:
In a war of the future, there would be no use whatever to say that "We must not use poison gas; we must not spread disease germs; we must not kill civilians; we must not have submarine warfare; we must not destroy hospital ships; we must not bomb hospitals; we must not drop bombs on undefended towns.
All tlies things will be done."
Well, if all these forms of warfare will be resorted to, if we were thoroughly consistent and were going to be prepared for the next war, instead of pottering away with a few soldiers and officers as we are doing to-day, we would be arming along those lines and preparing definitely to carry on a warfare of

I agree, we cannot, because there can be released enough germs, poison gas and so on to wipe out our cities in a very short time. If that be the case, why not let us frankly face the situation and attempt to discover some substitute for armament and prevent these disasters that will inevitably result from a war in the future.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION OP COMMISSION FOR ACQUISITION, OPERATION, REGULATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: I understand there has been some correspondence between the Canadian Legion, the British Empire Service League and the minister concerning the publication of the Canadian official history of the great war. Can the minister tell what progress is being made by the department in this connection?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: CONSTITUTION OP COMMISSION FOR ACQUISITION, OPERATION, REGULATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: This subject has created a great deal of interest, and rightly so. Practically ever since the war a subdepartment has been gathering information and data. To be useful, any history must be exact. If the hon. member is particularly interested and will come to my department I shall be very happy to show him how exact that information is. From the information at hand, the officials know all the details of a battle on a certain date at a certain hour, and they have the detailed information concerning the companies, squadrons and batteries. At a time six hours later there are further details to show the changes which have been made. That preliminary work has now reached the stage where it is possible to begin writing the history. Probably it will consist of eight or nine general volumes, and two or three in addition dealing with particular services. Work will be started on the first volume immediately. It must be remembered that there are two kinds of histories of the war. One is official, giving days and dates, and quoting orders; another deals with certain incidents and embellishes them in an effort to make the subject matter readable. Some writer may comment on whether or not he approved of a certain general, or the practice of protecting the infantry by artillery fire. That may be a readable history, but it is not official. On the other hand, the official history may be used as a ground work for writers who may direct their thoughts along general lines. I hope that before parliament meets next year one volume will be ready.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION OP COMMISSION FOR ACQUISITION, OPERATION, REGULATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: Is it not a fact that Great Britain, Australia and other parts of the British empire are ahead of Canada, so far as the histories of their respective parts in the war are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: CONSTITUTION OP COMMISSION FOR ACQUISITION, OPERATION, REGULATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
In some cases they have written the second type of history I have described, namely that prepared in sketchy and newsy form. Such histories, however, are not official. Great Britain is now writing her official history of the war, and it has been the practice of her officials to send to us anything concerning the Canadian troops, the information being checked by the officers in our 
department. Great Britain has begun work on the official history, but I would not admit that she is ahead of us in that particular work.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION OP COMMISSION FOR ACQUISITION, OPERATION, REGULATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
Apparently the officials in
charge of this work have been thirteen jmars gathering data. I notice in a return which was brought down on April 24, 1929, that at that time they had sorted 135 tons of material; indexed and made available documents occupying 3,138 feet of shelving; selected and copied documents covering 20,000 pages with maps; supplied information to inquirers on a wide variety of subjects necessitating writing approximately 8,000 letters; and compiled historical information comprising approximately 6,432 pages, 150 maps, 4,288 charts and 12,000 cards. To any ordinary layman who is interested in the subject this would appear to be sufficient data on which to base the history. I suppose I could go over to the department and see how the data is gathered, but the men most interested in this history are the veterans themselves, and many of them feel they will be dead before the history appears. I think it would be not unfair to say that the men in charge of this work have been dilatory, to say the least. I was very glad indeed to hear the minister suggest that we might perhaps expect one volume this year. Who is to be given the task of writing this history, the man who is in the department now and has been engaged on the work for the last fifteen years?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: CONSTITUTION OP COMMISSION FOR ACQUISITION, OPERATION, REGULATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: Colonel Duguid will write the history. He has been head of the sub-department for a number of years. I must correct the hon. gentleman when he suggests that Colonel Duguid or anyone else in that particular branch has been dilatory. He certainly has not been dilatory. He may not have been given the help he needed, but his is a very small branch. No one has worked harder, or put greater effort into the preparation of this history than has Colonel Duguid.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION OP COMMISSION FOR ACQUISITION, OPERATION, REGULATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: How many men are engaged in this work, and how much has been spent on it already? Has not sufficient work been done and money expended to justify our expectations that some of these volumes might have been published before this?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: CONSTITUTION OP COMMISSION FOR ACQUISITION, OPERATION, REGULATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
I do not think the hon. gentleman will find there is a great deal of dissatisfaction, for it must be remembered that it takes a long time to get exact information for the preparation of such a history. Several histories have been written in the older countries by some general or staff

Banking and Commerce-Report
officer giving his views on the strategy employed by the various generals. But that is not an official history in the sense in which we regard the history that is to be written for this country. Our history must be based on authentic information.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION OP COMMISSION FOR ACQUISITION, OPERATION, REGULATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: I desire to second what the minister has said with regard to Colonel Duguid's work. It may be, as the minister suggests, that Colonel Duguid himself may not have had sufficient help. I think it would be rather difficult for him to use very much help in view of the technical nature of the work he is doiug. I know that for several years while I was in the department he was still opening boxes and packages and collecting data which was coming in from all sources, and at the same time he was busy answering inquiries from those in several parts of the country who were writing battalion histories. Wonderful work was done by the historical section in connection with the memorial chamber in this building. If I remember correctly, with respect to the Canadian war memorial which is'now being prepared, a great many ideas, if not suggested, were at least forwarded by Colonel Duguid's work. Dilatory is the last word my hon. friend ought to apply to Colonel Duguid; I do not know one whose heart is more in his work or who is more industrious.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION OP COMMISSION FOR ACQUISITION, OPERATION, REGULATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: I do not know the gentleman at all, and it may be that he has done all he could do. Perhaps I should have said the department has been dilatory. At least that is the opinion of a great many returned men who are still looking for the official history of the war. As I have said, they are the men who are interested and many of them fear they will be dead before the history appears.
